paragraphs.speaker: BASSANIO.
paragraphs.proposed: BASSANIO. So outward shows may be the least like what they really are. The world is always deceived by ornament. In law, what plea is so tainted and corrupt that, seasoned with a charming voice, it can't hide its look of evil? In religion, what damnable error is there that some solemn-faced man won't bless and confirm with a text from scripture, hiding its grossness with fair ornament? There's no vice so simple-minded that it doesn't assume some mark of virtue on its outward parts. How many cowards, whose hearts are as treacherous as stairs of sand, still wear on their chins the beards of Hercules and frowning Mars, though, searched inside, they have livers as white as milk; and these put on only valor's outgrowth, a brave man's beard, to make themselves feared. Look at beauty, and you'll see it's bought by weight, and there it works a miracle in nature, making those who wear the most of it the lightest: light in weight, and light in virtue. In the same way, those curled, snaking golden locks that frolic so wantonly with the wind on the head of some supposed beauty often turn out to be the dowry of a second head: a wig, grown by a skull that now lies in the tomb. Thus ornament is only the treacherous shore of a most dangerous sea; the beautiful scarf that veils a dark Indian face and passes it off as a beauty; in a word, the seeming truth which cunning times put on to entrap the wisest. Therefore, you gaudy gold, hard food for Midas, whose every bite turned to gold, I'll have none of you. Nor any of you, silver, you pale and common drudge that passes between man and man as money. But you, you meager lead, which threatens rather than promises anything, your paleness moves me more than eloquence, and here I choose. May joy be the consequence!

units.o: So may the outward shows be least themselves.
units.m: So outward shows may be the least like what they really are.

units.o: The world is still deceiv’d with ornament.
units.m: The world is always deceived by ornament.

units.o: In law, what plea so tainted and corrupt / But, being season’d with a gracious voice, / Obscures the show of evil?
units.m: In law, what plea is so tainted and corrupt that, seasoned with a charming voice, it can't hide its look of evil?

units.o: In religion, / What damned error but some sober brow / Will bless it, and approve it with a text, / Hiding the grossness with fair ornament?
units.m: In religion, what damnable error is there that some solemn-faced man won't bless and confirm with a text from scripture, hiding its grossness with fair ornament?

units.o: There is no vice so simple but assumes / Some mark of virtue on his outward parts.
units.m: There's no vice so simple-minded that it doesn't assume some mark of virtue on its outward parts.

units.o: How many cowards, whose hearts are all as false / As stairs of sand, wear yet upon their chins / The beards of Hercules and frowning Mars,
units.m: How many cowards, whose hearts are as treacherous as stairs of sand, still wear on their chins the beards of Hercules and frowning Mars,

units.o: Who inward search’d, have livers white as milk,
units.m: though, searched inside, they have livers as white as milk;

units.o: And these assume but valour’s excrement / To render them redoubted.
units.m: and these put on only valor's outgrowth, a brave man's beard, to make themselves feared.

units.o: Look on beauty, / And you shall see ’tis purchas’d by the weight, / Which therein works a miracle in nature, / Making them lightest that wear most of it:
units.m: Look at beauty, and you'll see it's bought by weight, and there it works a miracle in nature, making those who wear the most of it the lightest: light in weight, and light in virtue.

units.o: So are those crisped snaky golden locks / Which make such wanton gambols with the wind / Upon supposed fairness, often known / To be the dowry of a second head, / The skull that bred them in the sepulchre.
units.m: In the same way, those curled, snaking golden locks that frolic so wantonly with the wind on the head of some supposed beauty often turn out to be the dowry of a second head: a wig, grown by a skull that now lies in the tomb.

units.o: Thus ornament is but the guiled shore / To a most dangerous sea;
units.m: Thus ornament is only the treacherous shore of a most dangerous sea;

units.o: the beauteous scarf / Veiling an Indian beauty;
units.m: the beautiful scarf that veils a dark Indian face and passes it off as a beauty;

units.o: in a word, / The seeming truth which cunning times put on / To entrap the wisest.
units.m: in a word, the seeming truth which cunning times put on to entrap the wisest.

units.o: Therefore thou gaudy gold, / Hard food for Midas, I will none of thee,
units.m: Therefore, you gaudy gold, hard food for Midas, whose every bite turned to gold, I'll have none of you.

units.o: Nor none of thee, thou pale and common drudge / ’Tween man and man:
units.m: Nor any of you, silver, you pale and common drudge that passes between man and man as money.

units.o: but thou, thou meagre lead, / Which rather threaten’st than dost promise aught, / Thy palenness moves me more than eloquence,
units.m: But you, you meager lead, which threatens rather than promises anything, your paleness moves me more than eloquence,

units.o: And here choose I, joy be the consequence!
units.m: and here I choose. May joy be the consequence!

reasons: L1 'least themselves' = least like what they really are; current 'the least like themselves' is opaque by ear. Johnson (in Furness, New Variorum Merchant of Venice (1888), note on III.ii.79): he begins abruptly, the first part of the argument having passed in his mind; 'So' kept.
L2 false friend fixed: 'still' = always (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), still adv.: 'always, ever, continually'); current 'is still deceived' is heard as 'even now'.

L3-5 unnatural syntax fixed: current 'what plea so tainted and corrupt that ... doesn't obscure' has no main verb. 'season'd' continues the spoiled-meat metaphor of 'tainted' (Clarendon in Furness, note on 82), so both words are kept; 'gracious' = attractive, lovely (Onions, gracious 2, citing this line) -> 'charming'; 'Obscures the show of evil' -> 'hide its look of evil'.

L5-8 hard idiom and metonymy made clear: 'What damned error but some sober brow / Will bless it' (archaic 'what ... but') -> 'what damnable error is there that some solemn-faced man won't bless'; 'approve' = prove, confirm (Onions approve 1, citing 'approve it with a text'; Dyce in Furness: 'ratify, confirm') and 'text' = a text from scripture; current left 'sober brow' and 'approve it with a text' untranslated. 'grossness' = flagrant character, enormity (Onions, citing this line): kept, since modern 'grossness' carries it.
L9-10 kept from current word for word ('vice' is the F1 reading followed by all editors from Rowe; the Quartos read 'voice', per Furness's collation).

L11-13 'false' = treacherous, giving way under the foot (Knight in Furness, note on 90: stairs of sand 'betray the feet of those who trust to them') -> 'as treacherous as stairs of sand'; current 'as false as staircases of sand'.

L14 hard image made clear: a white, bloodless liver is the sign of cowardice (Onions s.v. liver: 'white or pale l., symbolical of cowardice', citing this line). Current 'have livers white as milk' leaves the point to the listener, and its dashed aside attaches 'who' to Hercules and Mars; 'though ... they' fixes the reference.

L15-16 mis-gloss fixed: 'valour's excrement' = the beard, valour's outgrowth (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (Perseus) s.v. Excrement 2: 'that which grows out of the body, hair, beard ... assume but valour's e. (the beard of Hercules) Merch. III, 2, 87'; Onions: 'valour's e. (= a brave man's beard)'; Malone and Staunton in Furness). Current 'the mere outward show of valor' drops the beard image; 'redoubted' = feared.

L16-19 flattened pun restored: 'lightest' = least heavy and most wanton (Onions light adj. 3 'wanton, unchaste', 'quibbles are frequent'; Heath in Furness: 'the more it is laid on, the more lightness it indicates in the wearer'). Current keeps 'lightest' but the moral sense is inaudible; 'therein' archaic. Beauty bought 'by the weight' = cosmetics and false hair (Heath).

L20-24 hard image made clear: the golden locks are a wig made from a dead woman's hair (Malone in Furness on the periwig fashion); 'dowry' = property (Schmidt s.v. Dowry 2 'property (of women) in general', citing this line), kept with the gloss 'a wig'; 'crisped' = curled (Onions; Steevens); 'wanton gambols' = frolics (Onions wanton adj. 1); 'supposed' = pretended (Onions supposed 2); 'Upon supposed fairness' = surmounting a counterfeit beauty (Clarendon in Furness). Current left 'dowry of a second head' untranslated.

L25-26 'guiled' = treacherous, full of guile (Onions 'guiled: treacherous (S.)', citing this line; Schmidt s.v. Guiled 'furnished or armed with deceit, treacherous'; Steevens and Clarendon in Furness); current 'deceptive shore to a ... sea' is close but unidiomatic.

L26-27 hard image made clear, prejudice kept at the original's strength: Qq and F1 read 'an Indian beautie' (kept by most editors; Hanmer's 'dowdy', Keightley's 'feature' etc. rejected). 'Indian' is derogatory: a dark-skinned face that the speaker's world did not count as beauty (Brae and White in Furness; Furness: 'An Indian beauty is assuredly not an English beauty'). Current 'the beautiful scarf veiling an Indian beauty' leaves the listener unable to hear why the scarf deceives. The rendering neither softens nor sharpens: it says only what 'Indian beauty' carried.
L27-29 kept from current word for word ('seeming truth', 'cunning times' are clear).
L29-30 allusion made clear: Midas's food turned to gold at his touch; a five-word gloss added. 'I will none of thee' -> 'I'll have none of you' (current).

L31-32 hard image made clear: the 'pale and common drudge' is silver coin, a menial passing from hand to hand (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (Perseus) s.v. Drudge: 'one employed in mean service, a slave', citing Merch. III, 2, 103); current 'pale and common drudge between man and man' leaves both the metal and the money image unstated.

L32-34 textual crux recorded: Gutenberg's 'palenness' is a misprint. Chose 'paleness', the reading of Q1 ('palenes'), Q2 and F1 ('palenesse'), kept by Cambridge/Globe (not among Furness's 'plainness' editors); Warburton's emendation 'plainness' (favoured by Furness) is the alternative. Current dash removed.
L35 archaic optative 'joy be the consequence' -> 'May joy be the consequence!'.
Conventions: current's unspaced em dashes removed; American spelling kept as in the edition (valor, meager).

paragraphs.proposed: anxious thoughts, and despair embraced too rashly, and shuddering fear, and green-eyed jealousy. Oh, love, be moderate; calm your ecstasy. Rain your joy in due measure; restrain this excess! I feel too much of your blessing — make it less, for fear I overindulge and sicken.

units.o: As doubtful thoughts, and rash-embrac’d despair, / And shudd’ring fear, and green-ey’d jealousy.
units.m: anxious thoughts, and despair embraced too rashly, and shuddering fear, and green-eyed jealousy.

units.o: O love, be moderate; allay thy ecstasy, / In measure rain thy joy; scant this excess!
units.m: Oh, love, be moderate; calm your ecstasy. Rain your joy in due measure; restrain this excess!

units.o: I feel too much thy blessing, make it less, / For fear I surfeit.
units.m: I feel too much of your blessing — make it less, for fear I overindulge and sicken.

reasons: L1 'As' = to wit, namely (Furness, note on III.ii.115, citing Walker and Abbott §113). Current 'as doubtful thoughts' is heard as 'while' or 'because'; the list now follows the dash that ends 14.15.

L1 false friend fixed: 'doubtful' = apprehensive, suspicious (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), doubtful, citing Mer.V. III.ii.109) -> 'anxious thoughts'; current 'doubtful thoughts' is heard as 'uncertain'.
L1 compound unpacked: 'rash-embrac'd despair' -> 'despair embraced too rashly'. 'green-eyed jealousy' kept (clear, recognizable).

L3-4 unnatural syntax fixed: current 'In measure rain your joy' keeps the inverted order; 'measure' = moderation (Onions measure 4, citing 'In measure rain thy joy'). Textual crux recorded: 'rain' (F1 'raine'; Rowe and most editors after Malone) vs 'rein' (Singer, Collier, Cambridge, Globe; preferred by Clarendon and Furness). The served text reads 'rain' and the words sound the same aloud, so 'rain' is kept.
L5-6 image restored: 'surfeit' = sicken from too much food or drink; current 'for fear I'm overwhelmed' drops the feast image -> 'for fear I overindulge and sicken'. Dash spaced.

reviewer_fixes.find: Let your joy rain down in due measure;
reviewer_fixes.replace: Rain your joy in due measure;
reviewer_fixes.reason: 'rain down' closed the rain/rein crux that the current wording left open to the ear (F1 'raine', Q3 'reine'; Furness collation).

paragraphs.speaker: BASSANIO.
paragraphs.proposed: BASSANIO. What do I find here? [Opening the leaden casket.] Fair Portia's likeness! What demi-god of a painter has come so close to creating life? Do these eyes move? Or do they only seem to be in motion because they're riding on my own moving eyeballs? Here are parted lips, held apart by sugar-sweet breath: it's fitting that so sweet a barrier should part such sweet friends. Here in her hair the painter plays the spider, and has woven a golden mesh to trap the hearts of men faster and more firmly than gnats are caught in cobwebs. But her eyes! How could he see to paint them? Having painted one, I'd think it would have the power to steal both of his own eyes and leave itself without its partner. And yet, look: just as far as the substance of my praise wrongs this shadow, this painted image, by undervaluing it, so far does this shadow limp behind the substance, the living woman. Here's the scroll, which holds and sums up my fortune.

units.o: What find I here? [_Opening the leaden casket_.]
units.m: What do I find here? [Opening the leaden casket.]

units.o: Fair Portia’s counterfeit!
units.m: Fair Portia's likeness!

units.o: What demi-god / Hath come so near creation?
units.m: What demi-god of a painter has come so close to creating life?

units.o: Move these eyes? / Or whether, riding on the balls of mine, / Seem they in motion?
units.m: Do these eyes move? Or do they only seem to be in motion because they're riding on my own moving eyeballs?

units.o: Here are sever’d lips, / Parted with sugar breath, so sweet a bar / Should sunder such sweet friends.
units.m: Here are parted lips, held apart by sugar-sweet breath: it's fitting that so sweet a barrier should part such sweet friends.

units.o: Here in her hairs / The painter plays the spider, and hath woven / A golden mesh t’entrap the hearts of men / Faster than gnats in cobwebs.
units.m: Here in her hair the painter plays the spider, and has woven a golden mesh to trap the hearts of men faster and more firmly than gnats are caught in cobwebs.

units.o: But her eyes!— / How could he see to do them?
units.m: But her eyes! How could he see to paint them?

units.o: Having made one, / Methinks it should have power to steal both his / And leave itself unfurnish’d.
units.m: Having painted one, I'd think it would have the power to steal both of his own eyes and leave itself without its partner.

units.o: Yet look how far / The substance of my praise doth wrong this shadow / In underprizing it, so far this shadow / Doth limp behind the substance.
units.m: And yet, look: just as far as the substance of my praise wrongs this shadow, this painted image, by undervaluing it, so far does this shadow limp behind the substance, the living woman.

units.o: Here’s the scroll, / The continent and summary of my fortune.
units.m: Here's the scroll, which holds and sums up my fortune.

reasons: L1-2 kept from current ('counterfeit' = likeness, portrait: Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), citing this line; Steevens in Furness 'a likeness, without comprehending any idea of fraud'). Inline stage direction kept exactly as the current modern text has it.
L2-3 hard line made clear: the demi-god is the painter, who came near to creating a living woman; current 'has come so near to creation' is opaque by ear.

L3-5 image made clear: the painted eyes seem to move because Bassanio's own eyeballs carry them; 'Or whether' = or (Abbott §136, via Furness). Current 'riding on the balls of mine' is left close to the original and is opaque (and open to an unintended hearing) aloud.

L5-7 mis-gloss fixed: 'should' = ought (Furness, note on III.ii.127: 'In the sense of ought'); it is fitting that so sweet a bar parts such sweet friends. Current 'so sweet a barrier should ever sunder such sweet friends' turns the compliment into a reproach.

L7-10 false friend fixed: 'fast' in Shakespeare commonly = firmly fixed (Onions fast adj. 2 'firmly adhering'; he also notes the 'rapid, quick' sense occurs). Current 'faster than gnats in cobwebs' is heard only as 'more quickly'; both senses kept.
L10-11 'do them' = paint them; current's unspaced '!—' removed.

L11-13 mis-gloss fixed: 'unfurnish'd' = unmatched with its fellow, i.e. without the second eye (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), unfurnish'd, citing this line; Monck Mason and Henley in Furness). Current 'unfinished' reproduces Rowe's emendation (followed by Pope, Theobald, Warburton), not the Q/F word the original shows. 'should have power' = would have the power.

L13-16 wordplay made clear: shadow = the painted image, substance = the real Portia (the stock substance/shadow antithesis); 'how far ... so far' = 'as far as ... so far' (Abbott §46, via Furness). Current leaves 'shadow' and 'substance' untranslated; 'underprizing' -> 'undervaluing'.

L16-17 false friend fixed: 'continent' = that which contains (Dyce in Furness; Onions continent sb. 1) and, per Onions sb. 4, 'summary, sum' (citing this line); 'which holds and sums up' covers both. Current 'the content and summary' is a near miss.

structure_notes: 14.14-14.16: the parser split Portia's aside into three paragraphs: a lone speaker prefix 'PORTIA.' (14.14), the first verse line with its [Aside.] direction and no prefix (14.15), and the remaining five lines with no prefix (14.16). Fragment structure kept. 14.15 now ends with a spaced em dash, which stands for the original's 'As' (= namely); 14.16 continues in lower case.
14.17: the inline direction [Opening the leaden casket.] is kept exactly as the current modern text has it, after the first sentence.

14.13 line 34: Gutenberg prints 'palenness', a misprint. Proposed follows 'paleness' (Q1 'palenes', Q2/F1 'palenesse', kept by Cambridge/Globe per Furness's collation); Warburton's emendation 'plainness', which Furness (1888) favours, is the recorded alternative.

14.16 line 4: textual crux 'rain' (F1 'raine'; Rowe and most editors after Malone) vs 'rein' (Singer, Collier, Cambridge, Globe; preferred by Clarendon and Furness). Proposed follows the served text's 'rain'; the words sound the same aloud.

14.13 line 27: 'an Indian beauty' is the Qq/Ff reading, kept by most editors; Furness records many emendations (Hanmer 'dowdy', Keightley 'feature', Walker 'gipsy', etc.). Read with Brae, White and Furness as derogatory; see the reasons for 14.13.
Unit maps: o_lines are 1-based within the paragraph's Gutenberg lines; where a sentence boundary falls mid-line, adjacent units share that line, and the 'o' field quotes the exact original span.

14.13 L3-5: ungrammatical sentence ('what plea so tainted and corrupt that ... doesn't obscure' has no main verb).
14.13 L5-8: archaic 'what damned error, but some sober brow will bless it' construction left; 'sober brow' and 'approve it with a text' (approve = confirm, with a scripture text) untranslated.
14.13 L14: 'livers white as milk' left without its point (cowardice); the dashed aside attaches 'who' to Hercules and Mars.
14.13 L15-16: mis-gloss: 'valour's excrement' (= the beard) rendered 'the mere outward show of valor'; the beard image is lost.
14.13 L19: flattened pun: 'lightest' (light = unchaste) kept as a word, but the second sense is inaudible.
14.13 L20-24: 'the dowry of a second head' left untranslated; the listener cannot tell the curls are a wig of dead woman's hair.

14.13 L29-32: Midas allusion and 'pale and common drudge between man and man' (silver coin) left opaque.

Conventions: unspaced em dashes throughout ('Mars—who', 'breath—so', 'eyes!—how', 'anything—your', 'air—').

paragraphs.proposed: PORTIA. Please go through them one by one, and as you name them, I'll describe them, and from my description you can gauge my feelings.

units.o: I pray thee over-name them, and as thou namest them, I will describe them, and according to my description level at my affection.
units.m: Please go through them one by one, and as you name them, I'll describe them, and from my description you can gauge my feelings.

reasons: keep: meets the standard. 'level at' = guess at (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), level vb. 2, citing Mer.V. I.ii.41; the sense is transferred from 'aim'; Furness: 'aim at'); 'gauge my feelings' is an accurate modern equivalent.

paragraphs.speaker: PORTIA.
paragraphs.proposed: PORTIA. Yes, that one is a colt indeed, as giddy and witless as a young horse, for he does nothing but talk about his horse, and he counts it a great point in his favor that he can shoe it himself. I'm very much afraid her ladyship his mother was unfaithful with a blacksmith.

units.o: Ay, that’s a colt indeed, for he doth nothing but talk of his horse,
units.m: Yes, that one is a colt indeed, as giddy and witless as a young horse, for he does nothing but talk about his horse,

units.o: and he makes it a great appropriation to his own good parts that he can shoe him himself.
units.m: and he counts it a great point in his favor that he can shoe it himself.

units.o: I am much afeard my lady his mother play’d false with a smith.
units.m: I'm very much afraid her ladyship his mother was unfaithful with a blacksmith.

reasons: Mis-gloss fixed: 'Ay' = yes; current 'Ah' turns agreement into an interjection.

Flattened pun restored: 'colt' = a young horse and 'a witless, heady, gay youngster' (Johnson, in Furness, New Variorum Merchant of Venice (1888), note on I.ii.39); the horse-mad prince is both. Current keeps the word but only the horse sense is audible.

'appropriation to his own good parts' = special excellence added to his accomplishments (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), appropriation, citing I.ii.45; Singer in Furness): current 'a great point in his favor' kept.

Register restored: current 'had a fling' is modern slang (rule 6) and drops the mock-formal 'my lady his mother'; 'much afeard' = very much afraid, which current 'rather afraid' weakens; 'play'd false' = was unfaithful. The joke (he shoes horses because his real father was a smith) stays implicit, as in the original.
Convention: current's unspaced dash removed.

reviewer_fixes.reason: Keeps the mock formality and is clear by ear.

paragraphs.speaker: PORTIA.
paragraphs.proposed: PORTIA. He does nothing but frown, as if to say, “If you won't have me, choose as you please.” He hears funny stories and doesn't smile. I'm afraid he'll turn into the weeping philosopher when he gets old, being so full of ill-mannered gloom in his youth. I'd rather be married to a skull with a bone in its mouth than to either of those two. God protect me from them both!

units.o: He doth nothing but frown, as who should say “And you will not have me, choose.”
units.m: He does nothing but frown, as if to say, “If you won't have me, choose as you please.”

units.o: He hears merry tales and smiles not.
units.m: He hears funny stories and doesn't smile.

units.o: I fear he will prove the weeping philosopher when he grows old, being so full of unmannerly sadness in his youth.
units.m: I'm afraid he'll turn into the weeping philosopher when he gets old, being so full of ill-mannered gloom in his youth.

units.o: I had rather be married to a death’s-head with a bone in his mouth than to either of these.
units.m: I'd rather be married to a skull with a bone in its mouth than to either of those two.

units.o: God defend me from these two!
units.m: God protect me from them both!

reasons: Flattened double meaning restored: 'choose' = do as one likes (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), choose 1, citing 'An you will not have me, choose'; Schmidt via Furness: 'to do at one's pleasure'). Current 'suit yourself' has the sense but drops the word 'choose' on which the scene turns (Portia: 'O me, the word "choose"!'); 'choose as you please' keeps both.
False friend fixed: 'sadness' = seriousness (Onions, sadness); current 'unmannerly sadness' is heard as sorrow. 'already' in current was an addition and is removed.
Kept from current: 'funny stories', 'weeping philosopher' (Heraclitus, Clarendon in Furness; the phrase explains itself), 'skull with a bone in its mouth', 'God protect me from them both!'.
Convention: straight double quotes in current -> curly double quotes.

reviewer_fixes.reason: Schmidt files this line under Sadness 1 'sorrow, dejection', which makes him the future 'weeping philosopher'.

paragraphs.speaker: NERISSA.
paragraphs.proposed: NERISSA. What do you say about the French lord, Monsieur Le Bon?

units.o: How say you by the French lord, Monsieur Le Bon?
units.m: What do you say about the French lord, Monsieur Le Bon?

reasons: keep: 'How say you by' = what do you say about (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911) s.v. say, citing Mer.V. I.ii.57; Abbott §145 via Furness); correctly glossed.

paragraphs.speaker: PORTIA.
paragraphs.proposed: PORTIA. God made him, so let him pass for a man. Honestly, I know it's a sin to be a mocker, but him! Why, he has a better horse than the Neapolitan's, and a better bad habit of frowning than the Count Palatine. He's every man and no man at once. If a thrush sings, he immediately starts capering. He'd fence with his own shadow. If I married him, I'd be marrying twenty husbands. If he'd scorn me, I'd forgive him, because even if he loved me to madness, I could never return it.

units.o: God made him, and therefore let him pass for a man.
units.m: God made him, so let him pass for a man.

units.o: In truth, I know it is a sin to be a mocker, but he!
units.m: Honestly, I know it's a sin to be a mocker, but him!

units.o: why, he hath a horse better than the Neapolitan’s, a better bad habit of frowning than the Count Palatine.
units.m: Why, he has a better horse than the Neapolitan's, and a better bad habit of frowning than the Count Palatine.

units.o: He is every man in no man.
units.m: He's every man and no man at once.

units.o: If a throstle sing, he falls straight a-cap’ring.
units.m: If a thrush sings, he immediately starts capering.

units.o: He will fence with his own shadow.
units.m: He'd fence with his own shadow.

units.o: If I should marry him, I should marry twenty husbands.
units.m: If I married him, I'd be marrying twenty husbands.

units.o: If he would despise me, I would forgive him, for if he love me to madness, I shall never requite him.
units.m: If he'd scorn me, I'd forgive him, because even if he loved me to madness, I could never return it.

reasons: Flattened joke restored: 'a better bad habit of frowning' = he outdoes the Count even at a bad habit (Furness, note on I.ii.56-57: 'a better bad-habit'). Current 'a worse habit of frowning' (Halliwell's reading 'better bad = worse') breaks the 'better horse ... better bad habit' parallel that is the point: this suitor copies and outdoes every other.
All other sentences kept from current word for word ('throstle' = thrush; 'requite' = return his love).

paragraphs.speaker: NERISSA.
paragraphs.proposed: NERISSA. What do you say, then, to Falconbridge, the young baron of England?

units.o: What say you then to Falconbridge, the young baron of England?
units.m: What do you say, then, to Falconbridge, the young baron of England?

reasons: Flattened pun restored: Portia's reply 'I say nothing to him' plays on Nerissa's 'say ... to' (Clarendon in Furness, New Variorum Merchant of Venice (1888), note on I.ii.65: 'Portia playfully uses the phrase "say to" in a different sense from that which Nerissa meant'). Current 'What about Falconbridge' removes the phrase the joke needs, and drops 'then'.

paragraphs.speaker: PORTIA.
paragraphs.proposed: PORTIA. You know I say nothing to him, because he doesn't understand me, and I don't understand him. He has neither Latin, French, nor Italian, and you could go into court and swear that I have only a poor penny's worth of English. He's the portrait of a handsome man, but alas, who can hold a conversation with a mime? How oddly he's dressed! I think he bought his doublet in Italy, his puffed-out breeches in France, his hat in Germany, and his manners from everywhere.

units.o: You know I say nothing to him, for he understands not me, nor I him:
units.m: You know I say nothing to him, because he doesn't understand me, and I don't understand him.

units.o: he hath neither Latin, French, nor Italian, and you will come into the court and swear that I have a poor pennyworth in the English.
units.m: He has neither Latin, French, nor Italian, and you could go into court and swear that I have only a poor penny's worth of English.

units.o: He is a proper man’s picture; but alas, who can converse with a dumb-show?
units.m: He's the portrait of a handsome man, but alas, who can hold a conversation with a mime?

units.o: How oddly he is suited!
units.m: How oddly he's dressed!

units.o: I think he bought his doublet in Italy, his round hose in France, his bonnet in Germany, and his behaviour everywhere.
units.m: I think he bought his doublet in Italy, his puffed-out breeches in France, his hat in Germany, and his manners from everywhere.

reasons: Mis-gloss fixed: 'a poor pennyworth in the English' = a very small stock of English (Clarendon in Furness, New Variorum Merchant of Venice (1888), note on I.ii.67: 'You will bear me witness that I have but a very small stock of English'); current 'my English is worth only a penny' shifts the joke from quantity to value. 'you will come into the court and swear' = you are ready to testify (Abbott §320 via Furness) -> 'you could go into court and swear'.

False friend fixed: 'proper' = handsome (Steevens in Furness; Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), proper 5 'good-looking, handsome'); current 'a proper gentleman in a portrait' is heard as 'a respectable gentleman'.
Image restored: 'dumb-show' = a show in mime; current 'a silent picture' replaces it with a second picture image.

Archaic term made clear: 'round hose' = full, puffed breeches (Onions s.v. hose; Clarendon and Planché in Furness, note on I.ii.71: French hose 'made very round'); 'doublet' kept (familiar); 'bonnet' -> 'hat' (current).
Convention: current's unspaced dash removed.

paragraphs.speaker: NERISSA.
paragraphs.proposed: NERISSA. What do you think of the Scottish lord, his neighbor?

units.o: What think you of the Scottish lord, his neighbour?
units.m: What do you think of the Scottish lord, his neighbor?

reasons: keep: clear. The Gutenberg text follows the Quartos' 'Scottish'; F1 reads 'other' (Theobald in Furness: changed for fear of offending King James's countrymen).

paragraphs.speaker: PORTIA.
paragraphs.proposed: PORTIA. That he has a neighborly charity in him, for he borrowed a box on the ear from the Englishman, and swore he'd pay him back when he was able. I think the Frenchman became his guarantor, and set his seal under the bond for another box on the ear.

units.o: That he hath a neighbourly charity in him, for he borrowed a box of the ear of the Englishman, and swore he would pay him again when he was able.
units.m: That he has a neighborly charity in him, for he borrowed a box on the ear from the Englishman, and swore he'd pay him back when he was able.

units.o: I think the Frenchman became his surety, and seal’d under for another.
units.m: I think the Frenchman became his guarantor, and set his seal under the bond for another box on the ear.

reasons: Legal image made clear: 'seal'd under for another' = signed as surety beneath the principal, for another box on the ear (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), seal: 'seal under for, to become surety for', citing Mer.V. I.ii.88; Clarendon in Furness: 'The principal was said to "seal to" a bond; his surety "sealed under"'). Current 'went his guarantor, and signed on for another' is unnatural ('went') and vague ('signed on'). The allusion to France's promises of help to Scotland against England (Warburton in Furness) stays implicit, as in the original.
'pay him back' keeps the debt/revenge double sense (current, kept). Convention: current's unspaced dash replaced by 'for', the original's connective.

reviewer_fixes.find: set his seal under the bond for another one.
reviewer_fixes.replace: set his seal under the bond for another box on the ear.
reviewer_fixes.reason: 'another one' was heard as another bond; it means another box on the ear (Clarendon in Furness).

paragraphs.speaker: NERISSA.
paragraphs.proposed: NERISSA. How do you like the young German, the Duke of Saxony's nephew?

units.o: How like you the young German, the Duke of Saxony’s nephew?
units.m: How do you like the young German, the Duke of Saxony's nephew?

reasons: keep: clear.

paragraphs.speaker: PORTIA.
paragraphs.proposed: PORTIA. Very vilely in the morning, when he's sober, and most vilely in the afternoon, when he's drunk. At his best, he's a little worse than a man; at his worst, he's little better than a beast. And if the worst that ever happened should happen, I hope I can manage to do without him.

units.o: Very vilely in the morning when he is sober, and most vilely in the afternoon when he is drunk:
units.m: Very vilely in the morning, when he's sober, and most vilely in the afternoon, when he's drunk.

units.o: when he is best, he is a little worse than a man, and when he is worst, he is little better than a beast.
units.m: At his best, he's a little worse than a man; at his worst, he's little better than a beast.

units.o: And the worst fall that ever fell, I hope I shall make shift to go without him.
units.m: And if the worst that ever happened should happen, I hope I can manage to do without him.

reasons: Register and grammar restored: 'Very vilely' answers 'How like you' (I like him very vilely) and describes him at once; current 'Awful in the morning' is colloquial and does not answer the question.

Idiom made clear: 'And the worst fall that ever fell' = if the worst that ever happened should happen ('and' = if, Capell via Furness, New Variorum Merchant of Venice (1888); Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), fall 5 'to happen', citing this line); current 'whatever the worst that could happen' is awkward and loses the fall/fell echo, now carried by 'happened ... happen'. 'make shift' = manage (Onions, shift): current kept.
Middle sentence kept from current word for word.

paragraphs.speaker: NERISSA.
paragraphs.proposed: NERISSA. If he should offer to choose, and choose the right casket, you'd be refusing to perform your father's will if you refused to accept him.

units.o: If he should offer to choose, and choose the right casket, you should refuse to perform your father’s will, if you should refuse to accept him.
units.m: If he should offer to choose, and choose the right casket, you'd be refusing to perform your father's will if you refused to accept him.

reasons: keep: 'should' = would in the main clause (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), should 1, citing Mer.V. I.ii.98); correctly rendered.

paragraphs.speaker: PORTIA.
paragraphs.proposed: PORTIA. Therefore, for fear of the worst, please set a deep glass of Rhine wine on the wrong casket, because if the devil were inside it and that temptation outside, I know he'd choose it. I'll do anything, Nerissa, before I'll marry a sponge that soaks up drink.

units.o: Therefore, for fear of the worst, I pray thee set a deep glass of Rhenish wine on the contrary casket,
units.m: Therefore, for fear of the worst, please set a deep glass of Rhine wine on the wrong casket,

units.o: for if the devil be within and that temptation without, I know he will choose it.
units.m: because if the devil were inside it and that temptation outside, I know he'd choose it.

units.o: I will do anything, Nerissa, ere I will be married to a sponge.
units.m: I'll do anything, Nerissa, before I'll marry a sponge that soaks up drink.

reasons: Misreading fixed: 'if the devil be within and that temptation without' = inside and outside the casket on which the glass is set, i.e. even with the devil himself inside it, the wine on top would make him pick it. Current 'if there's a devil inside him' invents a referent and breaks the within/without pair.
Clear line restored: 'for fear of the worst' is already plain modern English and echoes her 'worst fall' just before; current 'just to be safe' changes it for no gain.
'Rhenish' = Rhine wine (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), Rhenish, citing I.ii.102); 'contrary' = wrong (Onions, contrary, citing this line): current kept.

Hard image made clear: 'sponge' = a drunkard who soaks up drink (Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon (Perseus) s.v. Sponge: 'a soft porous substance imbibing fluids: Merch. I, 2, 108'; Onions, spongy 1 'drunken', cf. Mer.V. I.ii.106). Today 'sponge' is heard as a freeloader, so the drink sense is made explicit.

structure_notes: 2.7-2.21 are single prose speeches with no parser fragments; unit maps are sentence-level (o_lines [1, 1], exact original span in 'o').
2.10 vs 2.13: the original itself has 'County Palatine' (Nerissa) and 'Count Palatine' (Portia); both are the same title (Malone in Furness), so the proposed text uses 'Count Palatine' in both.
2.16: the served text follows the Quartos' 'Scottish lord'; F1 reads 'other Lord'.
current_defects: 2.9: 'Ay' (yes) mis-rendered as 'Ah'; 'colt' pun (young horse / witless youngster) flattened; register: 'had a fling' is modern slang, 'rather afraid' weakens 'much afeard', mock-formal 'my lady his mother' dropped.
2.10: false friend: 'County Palatine' (county = count) left; heard as a territory.
2.11: 'unmannerly sadness' (sadness = seriousness) left as a false friend; 'suit yourself' drops the word 'choose' the scene turns on; 'already' added; straight double quotes.
2.13: flattened joke: 'a better bad habit of frowning' turned into 'a worse habit', breaking the 'better horse ... better bad habit' parallel.
2.14: flattened pun: 'What about Falconbridge' removes Nerissa's 'say ... to', which Portia's 'I say nothing to him' plays on.

2.15: 'a proper gentleman' (proper = handsome) left as a false friend; 'dumb-show' changed to 'a silent picture'; 'round hose' left opaque; 'my English is worth only a penny' shifts 'a poor pennyworth' (a small stock) from quantity to value.
2.17: 'went his guarantor' unnatural; 'signed on for another' blurs 'sealed under for another' (signed as surety, for another box on the ear).
2.19: 'Awful' does not answer 'How do you like' and is colloquial; 'whatever the worst that could happen' awkward.

2.21: misreading: 'a devil inside him' (within/without refer to the casket); 'just to be safe' needlessly replaces the clear 'for fear of the worst'; 'sponge' (drunkard) left where modern ears hear 'freeloader'; 'Rhenish' opaque.

paragraphs.speaker: SALARINO.
paragraphs.proposed: SALARINO. That's certain, if the devil may be her judge.

units.o: That’s certain, if the devil may be her judge.
units.m: That's certain, if the devil may be her judge.

reasons: keep: clear; the jab (Shylock as the devil judging her) stays implicit, as in the original.

paragraphs.speaker: SHYLOCK.
paragraphs.proposed: SHYLOCK. My own flesh and blood to rebel!

units.o: My own flesh and blood to rebel!
units.m: My own flesh and blood to rebel!

reasons: keep: clear, and the word 'rebel' is needed for Solanio's twist in 13.16.

paragraphs.speaker: SOLANIO.
paragraphs.proposed: SOLANIO. Shame on it, old carrion flesh! Is it still rebelling with lust at your age?

units.o: Out upon it, old carrion!
units.m: Shame on it, you old carrion!

units.o: Rebels it at these years?
units.m: Is your flesh still rebelling with lust at your age?

reasons: Flattened pun restored: Solanio twists Shylock's 'flesh and blood ... rebel' (his daughter) into Shylock's own flesh rebelling, i.e. lust, at his age. 'old carrion' = the living body, the flesh, used contemptuously (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), carrion (ii), citing 'Out upon it, old carrion! rebels it at these years?'). Current 'Are you still in heat at your age?' keeps only the explanation, drops 'rebel', and coarsens it to an animal-in-heat image the original does not use (rule 5).
'Out upon it' = shame on it; current 'Out on it' is archaic. The insult 'old carrion' is kept at full strength.

reviewer_fixes.find: Shame on it, you old carrion! Is your flesh still rebelling with lust at your age?
reviewer_fixes.replace: Shame on it, old carrion flesh! Is it still rebelling with lust at your age?
reviewer_fixes.reason: 'old carrion' is Shylock's flesh, the 'it' that rebels (Onions carrion 2(ii); Schmidt, Carrion 3).

paragraphs.speaker: SHYLOCK.
paragraphs.proposed: SHYLOCK. I say my daughter is my flesh and my blood.

units.o: I say my daughter is my flesh and my blood.
units.m: I say my daughter is my flesh and my blood.

reasons: keep: clear.

paragraphs.speaker: SALARINO.
paragraphs.proposed: SALARINO. There's more difference between your flesh and hers than between black jet and white ivory; more between your bloods than there is between red wine and white Rhine wine. But tell us, have you heard whether Antonio has had any loss at sea or not?

units.o: There is more difference between thy flesh and hers than between jet and ivory,
units.m: There's more difference between your flesh and hers than between black jet and white ivory;

units.o: more between your bloods than there is between red wine and Rhenish.
units.m: more between your bloods than there is between red wine and white Rhine wine.

units.o: But tell us, do you hear whether Antonio have had any loss at sea or no?
units.m: But tell us, have you heard whether Antonio has had any loss at sea or not?

reasons: Insult made understandable at its original strength: jet is black and ivory white; Rhenish (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911): 'Rhine wine') is white wine against red. Salarino's colour contrast between Shylock and Jessica is the point, and current 'jet and ivory ... red wine and Rhenish' leaves it inaudible to a modern listener. The colour words only name what the original's images already say; nothing is added to the insult.
Last sentence kept from current word for word.

paragraphs.speaker: SHYLOCK.
paragraphs.proposed: SHYLOCK. There I have another bad bargain: a bankrupt, a prodigal, who hardly dares show his head on the Rialto, a beggar who used to come to the marketplace so spruce and trim. Let him look to his bond. He used to call me usurer — let him look to his bond. He used to lend money out of Christian courtesy, free of interest — let him look to his bond.

units.o: There I have another bad match, a bankrupt, a prodigal, who dare scarce show his head on the Rialto, a beggar that used to come so smug upon the mart;
units.m: There I have another bad bargain: a bankrupt, a prodigal, who hardly dares show his head on the Rialto, a beggar who used to come to the marketplace so spruce and trim.

units.o: let him look to his bond.
units.m: Let him look to his bond.

units.o: He was wont to call me usurer; let him look to his bond:
units.m: He used to call me usurer — let him look to his bond.

units.o: he was wont to lend money for a Christian cur’sy; let him look to his bond.
units.m: He used to lend money out of Christian courtesy, free of interest — let him look to his bond.

reasons: Mis-gloss fixed: 'match' = bargain, compact (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), match 3, citing 'another bad match', Mer.V. III.i.48); current 'bad match' is heard as a marriage or a contest.

False friend fixed: 'smug' = neat, spruce, trim (Onions, smug, citing 'to come so smug upon the mart', III.i.51); current 'so smug upon the market' is heard as 'self-satisfied' and 'upon the market' is unidiomatic.

Point made clear: lending 'for a Christian cur'sy' = as a Christian courtesy, without interest (Edwards in Furness, New Variorum Merchant of Venice (1888), note on III.i.41: his lending without interest is why Shylock calls him prodigal); two-word gloss added.
Natural order: 'dares scarcely show' -> 'hardly dares show'. The refrain 'let him look to his bond' is kept as the recognizable threat. Dashes spaced.

paragraphs.speaker: SALARINO.
paragraphs.proposed: SALARINO. Why, I'm sure if he forfeits, you won't take his flesh! What's that good for?

units.o: Why, I am sure if he forfeit, thou wilt not take his flesh! What’s that good for?
units.m: Why, I'm sure if he forfeits, you won't take his flesh! What's that good for?

reasons: keep: 'forfeit' = fail to keep an obligation (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), forfeit vb., citing Mer.V. III.i.55); 'if he forfeits' is clear in the context of the bond.

paragraphs.speaker: SHYLOCK.
paragraphs.proposed: SHYLOCK. To bait fish with. If it feeds nothing else, it will feed my revenge. He has disgraced me, and cost me half a million, laughed at my losses, mocked at my gains, scorned my nation, thwarted my deals, cooled my friends, heated my enemies. And what's his reason? I am a Jew. Has not a Jew eyes? Has not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions? Fed with the same food, hurt by the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer as a Christian is? If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die? And if you wrong us, shall we not revenge? If we are like you in the rest, we will resemble you in that. If a Jew wrongs a Christian, what is his humility? Revenge. If a Christian wrongs a Jew, what should his patient endurance be, by Christian example? Why, revenge! The villainy you teach me I will execute, and it will take a great deal to stop me from improving on the instruction.

units.o: To bait fish withal; if it will feed nothing else, it will feed my revenge.
units.m: To bait fish with. If it feeds nothing else, it will feed my revenge.

units.o: He hath disgrac’d me and hind’red me half a million, laugh’d at my losses, mock’d at my gains, scorned my nation, thwarted my bargains, cooled my friends, heated mine enemies.
units.m: He has disgraced me, and cost me half a million, laughed at my losses, mocked at my gains, scorned my nation, thwarted my deals, cooled my friends, heated my enemies.

units.o: And what’s his reason? I am a Jew.
units.m: And what's his reason? I am a Jew.

units.o: Hath not a Jew eyes? Hath not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions?
units.m: Has not a Jew eyes? Has not a Jew hands, organs, dimensions, senses, affections, passions?

units.o: Fed with the same food, hurt with the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer as a Christian is?
units.m: Fed with the same food, hurt by the same weapons, subject to the same diseases, healed by the same means, warmed and cooled by the same winter and summer as a Christian is?

units.o: If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die? And if you wrong us, shall we not revenge?
units.m: If you prick us, do we not bleed? If you tickle us, do we not laugh? If you poison us, do we not die? And if you wrong us, shall we not revenge?

units.o: If we are like you in the rest, we will resemble you in that.
units.m: If we are like you in the rest, we will resemble you in that.

units.o: If a Jew wrong a Christian, what is his humility? Revenge.
units.m: If a Jew wrongs a Christian, what is his humility? Revenge.

units.o: If a Christian wrong a Jew, what should his sufferance be by Christian example? Why, revenge!
units.m: If a Christian wrongs a Jew, what should his patient endurance be, by Christian example? Why, revenge!

units.o: The villainy you teach me I will execute, and it shall go hard but I will better the instruction.
units.m: The villainy you teach me I will execute, and it will take a great deal to stop me from improving on the instruction.

reasons: Archaic idiom made clear: 'it shall go hard but I will' = I will assuredly, unless overwhelming difficulties prevent it (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911) s.v. hard: 'go h. but introduces a statement of what will happen unless overwhelming difficulties prevent it, esp. it shall go h. but I will = I will assuredly', citing Mer.V. III.i.78). Current leaves 'it shall go hard but' untranslated. Current's unspaced dash replaced by the original's comma.

Everything else kept from current word for word, including the famous lines. 'hindered me half a million' -> current 'cost me half a million' is a fair gloss (Abbott §198a via Furness). 'humility' kept: Schmidt (quoted in Furness, note on III.i.62) glosses it 'kindness, benevolence, humanity', but the modern sense (Christian meekness) carries the same irony, so the famous line stays recognizable. 'dimensions' = bodily frame (Onions) and 'organs' = members of the body (Onions) are clear enough in the list.

reviewer_fixes.replace: what should his patient endurance be
reviewer_fixes.reason: Restores the echo of 'sufferance is the badge of all our tribe' (I.iii; live text 'endurance').

units.m: [Enter a man from Antonio.]

paragraphs.speaker: SHYLOCK.
paragraphs.proposed: SHYLOCK. Well, Tubal, what news from Genoa? Have you found my daughter?

units.o: How now, Tubal, what news from Genoa? Hast thou found my daughter?
units.m: Well, Tubal, what news from Genoa? Have you found my daughter?

reasons: Archaic idiom made clear: 'How now' (an old greeting and call for news) -> 'Well'; the rest kept from current.

paragraphs.speaker: TUBAL.
paragraphs.proposed: TUBAL. I often came to places where I heard of her, but I can't find her.

units.o: I often came where I did hear of her, but cannot find her.
units.m: I often came to places where I heard of her, but I can't find her.

reasons: Natural syntax and tense: 'came where I did hear of her' -> 'came to places where I heard of her'; 'cannot find her' is present (he still can't), which current 'couldn't' changes.

paragraphs.speaker: SHYLOCK.
paragraphs.proposed: SHYLOCK. Why, there it goes, there, there, there! A diamond gone that cost me two thousand ducats in Frankfurt! The curse never fell upon our nation until now — I never felt it until now. Two thousand ducats in that, and other precious, precious jewels. I wish my daughter were dead at my feet, with the jewels in her ear; I wish she were buried at my feet, with the ducats in her coffin. No news of them? Why so? And I don't know what's been spent in the search. Why, you — loss upon loss! The thief gone with so much, and so much spent to find the thief, and no satisfaction, no revenge, no ill luck stirring but what lands on my shoulders, no sighs but the ones I breathe, no tears but the ones I shed.

units.o: The thief gone with so much, and so much to find the thief, and no satisfaction, no revenge, nor no ill luck stirring but what lights o’ my shoulders, no sighs but o’ my breathing, no tears but o’ my shedding.
units.m: The thief gone with so much, and so much spent to find the thief, and no satisfaction, no revenge, no ill luck stirring but what lands on my shoulders, no sighs but the ones I breathe, no tears but the ones I shed.

reasons: False friend fixed: 'there, there, there, there' is heard today as comfort; Shylock's is exasperation at loss (his next words: 'A diamond gone'). 'there it goes' makes it audible while keeping the repetition.

Archaic wish made clear and consistent: current 'would she were hearsed' is left untranslated after 'I wish'; 'hearsed' = coffined, buried (Onions, A Shakespeare Glossary (1911), hearsed, citing Mer.V. III.i.96). The wish is kept at full brutality. 'at my foot' -> 'at my feet' (the modern idiom).

Garble fixed: 'no sighs but o' my breathing, no tears but o' my shedding' = no sighs but those I breathe, no tears but those I shed (Q1 'but of', followed by Cambridge and Globe, per Furness, New Variorum Merchant of Venice (1888)); current 'no sighs but my breathing, no tears but my shedding' makes breathing itself a sigh. 'lights' = lands (Onions, light vb.1 'to fall, descend'). 'ill luck' kept, because Tubal and Shylock echo it in 13.31-13.32. 'so much to find the thief' = so much spent: one-word gloss.
Addition removed: current 'I don't even know' adds 'even'.

Textual cruxes recorded, served-text readings kept: 'Why so?' is printed as a question in F1 and in the served text, and Furness prefers the question ('Why is there no news of them?'); Johnson and Capell print 'why, so', and Onions reads 'why, so!' = 'well, so let it be' (s.v. why, citing III.i.98). 'Why, thou—loss upon loss!' is the Q/F1 'thou' with Collier's dash; the later Folios read 'then', which Furness thinks right. Kept open as 'Why, you — loss upon loss!'.
Conventions: dashes spaced.

paragraphs.proposed: SHYLOCK. I thank you, good Tubal. Good news, good news! Ha, ha — heard in Genoa?

units.m: I thank you, good Tubal. Good news, good news! Ha, ha — heard in Genoa?

reasons: keep: wording meets the standard. Crux recorded: 'heard in Genoa?' is the served (Gutenberg) reading; Qq and Ff read 'here in Genoa', Rowe and later editors 'where? in Genoa?' (Furness, New Variorum Merchant of Venice (1888), note on III.i.101). All three ask Tubal to confirm where the news came from, so the served reading stands. Unspaced dash: see structure_notes ('Ha, ha — heard').

paragraphs.proposed: TUBAL. Your daughter spent, as I heard, in Genoa, in one night, eighty ducats.

paragraphs.speaker: SHYLOCK.
paragraphs.proposed: SHYLOCK. You stick a dagger in me. I'll never see my gold again. Eighty ducats at one sitting! Eighty ducats!

units.m: You stick a dagger in me. I'll never see my gold again. Eighty ducats at one sitting! Eighty ducats!

reasons: keep: clear and forceful.

structure_notes: 13.22, 13.25 and 13.27 are stage directions, reproduced exactly as the current modern text has them (13.27 reads 'Exit' where the original has 'Exeunt'; left unchanged per the brief).
13.31/13.33: Tubal's sentence is interrupted by Shylock (13.32); the paragraph-final and paragraph-initial dashes are kept.

Edition-wide convention: the live MV modern-en uses unspaced em dashes ('Genoa—', 'Ha, ha—heard', 'usurer—let', 'execute—and', 'tribe—a', 'now—I', 'you—loss', '—had') and, in 2.11, straight double quotes; rule 8 requires spaced em dashes and curly double quotes. Every rewritten paragraph here follows rule 8. Kept paragraphs are reproduced word for word; 13.31 and 13.36 need only mechanical dash spacing ('Genoa —', 'Ha, ha — heard').
13.36: 'heard in Genoa?' is the served (Gutenberg) reading; Qq and Ff read 'here in Genoa', Rowe and most editors 'where? in Genoa?' (Furness). Kept, since the sense is the same.

13.30: 'Why so?' (a question in F1 and the served text, preferred by Furness) kept; Onions reads 'why, so!' as acquiescence. 'Why, thou—loss upon loss!' (Q/F1 'thou', Collier's dash) kept; the later Folios' 'then' is Furness's preference.
13.19-13.38 are prose; unit maps are sentence-level (o_lines [1, 1], exact original span in 'o').
current_defects: 13.16: flattened pun and coarsening: 'Are you still in heat at your age?' drops 'rebel' (Solanio's twist on Shylock's word) and swaps 'old carrion ... rebels it' for an animal-in-heat image.
13.18: 'jet and ivory', 'red wine and Rhenish' left, so the black/white colour contrast carrying the insult is inaudible.
13.19: mis-gloss 'bad match' (= bargain); false friend 'smug' (= spruce, trim); 'Christian courtesy' (lending without interest) left unexplained; 'dares scarcely show' unnatural order.
13.21: archaic idiom 'it shall go hard but I will' left untranslated.
13.26: 'a third one can't be matched' unclear by ear; subjunctive 'turn Jew' left.
13.28: archaic 'How now' left.
13.29: 'came where I heard of her' unnatural; 'couldn't find her' changes present 'cannot'.
13.30: 'there, there, there, there' left (heard today as comfort); 'would she were hearsed' left archaic after 'I wish'; 'no sighs but my breathing, no tears but my shedding' garbled; 'even' added.
13.33: 'argosy' (largest merchant ship) reduced to 'a merchant ship'; 'had ... lost' shifts 'hath ... cast away' into the past.
Conventions: unspaced em dashes in 13.19, 13.21, 13.26, 13.30, 13.31, 13.33, 13.36.
